title.en: Language work for Limitless Possibilities: modal functions, reported speech, collocations and slogans

text.en: Dr. Deepa Malik's journey and the poem Nine Gold Medals show how courage reshapes possibilities. In grammar, modal verbs fine-tune what is possible or advised, reported speech quotes inspiring interviews accurately, and strong collocations build memorable slogans.

keepEnglishTerms: Functions of would: request & past habit

text.en:
Unit 5 begins with five action idioms: 'defy the odds' means succeed when most people expect failure, while 'turn obstacles into stepping stones' means overcome difficulties to reach goals.
Compare the other three phrases: 'a new lease of life' means becoming more energetic and active than earlier; 'in hindsight' means understanding events after they happen; 'breakthrough moment' means a turning point of major discovery.
Modal auxiliaries express subtle shades of meaning depending on context. Notice that the exact same modal word can serve multiple distinct functions.
In the Kaveri modal table, 'could' expresses possibility, unreal ability, a polite request, or a constructive suggestion, whereas 'couldn't' marks past or present inability.
Similarly, 'should' expresses either sensible advice ('You should warm up before running') or probability ('They should reach the stadium by six').
Meanwhile, 'would' handles polite requests ('Would you pass the baton?') as well as recurring past habits ('Every morning she would train by the river').
In Unit 5 reported speech on Dr. Malik's interview, note how declarative sentences report without quotes using 'that': 'You've been listed' becomes 'she had been listed'.
Observe the verb shift carefully: simple present ('I love sports') becomes simple past ('she loved sports'), and simple past ('I decided') shifts back to past perfect ('had decided').
Crucially, check the exception in 'Dr. Malik: I believe youth is the voice of tomorrow': when the reporting verb is present ('Dr. Malik says that she believes'), tenses inside the report do NOT backshift!
Unit 5 reinforces noun-adjective collocations from 'Nine Gold Medals' such as 'standing ovation'. Good collocations pair 'heavy rain', 'strong wind', 'big disappointment/decision', 'large crowd' and 'great achievement'.
Watch closely for natural adjective upgrades too: instead of 'littlest athlete' or 'smiling attitude', Kaveri asks you to substitute sharper words like 'youngest athlete' and 'positive attitude'.
When practising interviews in the Speaking Activity, match register to listener: friendly openings ('Tell me about your love for sports') fit the School Captain, while formal requests ('It is my privilege...') fit the Sports Coach.
For the Listen and Respond school assembly task, predict what category fits each blank before listening—for instance a venue name, an inclusion theme, or an activity word.
Finally, Unit 5 teaches slogan writing on Special Athletes: keep ideas crisp, uplifting and memorable, using short parallel phrases and vivid action verbs.

problem.en: Change to reported speech and identify the modal function: (a) Tarun said, 'I will watch this documentary next weekend.' (b) 'We would train at dawn every winter.'

text.en: (a) Tarun said that he would watch that documentary the following weekend.

why.en: Simple future 'will' shifts to 'would', 'I' becomes 'he', and 'this... next weekend' becomes 'that... the following weekend'.
Repeating past routine actions without 'used to' uses 'would' for past habit.

prompt.en: Give three different functions of modal auxiliaries from Unit 5 and state why 'Dr. Malik says she believes...' does not change verb tense.

requiredIdeas.en: could shows possibility, request, suggestion or unreal ability; should shows advice or probability; would shows request or past habit
When the reporting verb is in the present tense (says), the reported verb keeps its original tense
had been and had decided show backshift when reporting verb is in past tense (said)

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking every modal has only one meaning
Changing present verbs to past after 'says that'

points.en: Key phrases: defy the odds, a new lease of life, in hindsight, breakthrough moment, turn obstacles into stepping stones.
Modals carry multiple functions: could (ability/request/possibility/suggestion), should (advice/probability), would (request/past habit).
Reported statements use reporting verbs + that, backshifting after past 'said' but keeping tense unchanged after present 'says'.
Adjective-noun collocations (heavy rain, strong wind, positive attitude, standing ovation) make speech and slogans natural.
